recommendation_issues.problem: The recommendation fixes React Router 8 while open question 1 leaves the router choice to the owner; it should not do both. React Router moved to a yearly major release cadence (v8 on 2026-06-17), and v8 needs React 19.2.7 or newer, so the panel can never share the phone's React 19.2.3 (Expo SDK 57) through one pinned version. TanStack Router has stayed on 1.x since 1.0.0 on 2023-12-23 (now 1.170.41, npm), accepts React 18 or newer, has 3 npm maintainers and comes from the same TanStack org as Query. Present both with these trade-offs and let the owner pick; the plan line names the router once chosen.

Serving the built panel through @fastify/static from the API image goes against Fastify's own Recommendations page (exposing Fastify directly is an anti-pattern; TLS termination and static files belong on a reverse proxy) and the @fastify/static README ('Production sites should use a reverse-proxy to manage caching headers'). The plan names no TLS terminator, and the panel needs HTTPS. Make it conditional: the proxy in front serves the static panel on the same origin and no Node plugin is added; @fastify/static only if that proxy cannot serve files. Dropping @fastify/cors holds either way.

The recommendation says what to write and where to test, but not what to do if Chrome 109 lecture PCs exist. Vite accepts a browser target such as 'chrome109' in build.target (per vite.dev/config/build-options, custom targets can be 'a browser with version (e.g. chrome58)'; Oxc lowers the syntax and warns on what it cannot lower). That fallback costs no package; @vitejs/plugin-legacy should not be added for this, and newer browser APIs must be avoided on the projection page.

misses.plan_quote: Projeksiyon sayfası (Aşama 2): eşleştirme koduyla açılır, yalnız QR'ı tam ekran gösterir.
misses.finding: The pairing code is made on the hoca's phone and typed into the lecture PC, and that PC's screen is what the projector shows (lines 241 and 863), so the whole room can read the code. The plan does not make the code single-use or bind it to one browser, and the paired page stays live until the lecture ends. Anyone who types the code on another device while it is valid gets the same rotating QR from the server and can scan it from home with a live camera. The delay stays far below the plan's 10 second 'normal' limit (line 243), so Aşama 2's proof of presence is bypassed without an accomplice in the room. Making the code single-use alone still leaves a race while the hoca types it. The OAuth device flow (RFC 8628) solves this exact case: the device that needs access shows a user code, the signed-in user approves it on their own device, and only the device holding the secret device code receives the token, so an onlooker gains nothing. The hoca's phone already scans QR codes (makbuz, line 431), so no new capability or package is needed.

misses.finding: Hoca sessions stay open for up to 30 days on up to 3 devices with no inactivity limit (line 69), and the panel is meant for any browser, including the shared lecture PCs the plan already relies on (lines 241, 863). A hoca who signs in on a lecture PC to check a list and walks away leaves a session the next user can open to approve suspicious records or change attendance. The 30-day rule matches NIST AAL1, where an inactivity timeout is optional, but the plan targets OWASP ASVS 5.0 level 2 (line 598), and its 7.3.1 requires an inactivity timeout set by risk analysis; shared PCs are exactly that risk. Better Auth's email-code sign-in takes only email, otp, name and image and has no 'remember me' switch (the email and password sign-in has one), so a shorter panel rule must be written on purpose.

misses.finding: The panel's page language is never set, and Vite's React template ships <html lang="en">. WCAG 2.2 3.1.1 (level A) requires the page language to be set so screen readers load the right pronunciation rules; with 'en', NVDA or VoiceOver read the Turkish panel with English rules, which breaks the screen reader support this line promises. CSS text-transform also follows the lang attribute: Turkish pairs i with İ and ı with I, so with 'en' uppercase labels turn 'i' into 'I'. The plan cares about I/ı and İ/i elsewhere (line 72), and S13-09 does not name this trap.

misses.finding: Times are stored in UTC (line 624), but the panel's display and export time zone is not fixed. Intl.DateTimeFormat uses the computer's own time zone unless one is given, SheetJS interprets dates by local time by default, and input type=date shows dates in the browser's locale (an English Chrome shows month first). A lecture PC or a laptop with a wrong zone or an English locale shifts session times and the edges of a report's date range, or invites a wrong date pick.

verdict_reason: I re-checked all 14 findings against their own sources and against independent primary sources (npm registry, W3C, WHATWG, MDN BCD, Vite, Fastify, SheetJS, Microsoft, Google, Expo, RFC 8628, OWASP ASVS). Result: 13 CONFIRMED and 1 CORRECTED. S13-08 is the corrected one: a TLS reverse proxy should serve the static panel, with @fastify/static only as the fallback, and 10.1.5 was published on 2026-09-26. Nothing was refuted or left unverifiable. I spot-checked all 17 checked_ok items (versions, dates, CVE fix versions, browser support, WCAG dates) and found no disputes. Three recommendations have wording or scope issues: S13-07, S13-08 and S13-06. The slice still FAILS because of one high-severity miss at line 447. The projection pairing code is typed on a lecture PC whose screen is projected. It is neither single-use nor bound to one browser, so anyone who reads it can stream the live rotating QR from home and pass the 10-second check, which defeats Aşama 2's proof of presence. The RFC 8628 reverse flow fixes this with no new package. Two medium misses remain. Panel sessions on shared lecture PCs have no inactivity timeout (ASVS 5.0 7.3.1, and Better Auth's email OTP has no remember-me). The page language is not set (Vite template ships lang=en; WCAG 3.1.1; Turkish i/İ casing). There are two low misses: the time zone and date format are left to the browser, and no QR generator is named. Process note: one read-only npm downloads lookup ran through curl in Bash instead of npm view. The same figures are at the cited api.npmjs.org URLs.
